analysis.one_liner: Stops Medicaid from taking deceased patients' family homes and estates to recover care costs.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 24 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since January 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently requires every state Medicaid program to try to claw back the cost of care after a beneficiary dies, by filing claims against their estate and placing liens on property like a family home. This bill repeals that requirement outright, bars any new recovery efforts, and orders states to withdraw existing liens and notify affected families within 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and surviving family members of people who received Medicaid — especially those who inherit a home. Because Medicaid covers long-term care that regularly affects middle-income seniors, estate recovery often forces the sale of the family house to repay the state. The bill ends that, including for liens already on homes today.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal requirement that states run a Medicaid Estate Recovery Program, ending claims against estates for correctly paid medical assistance.
Bars states from initiating, maintaining, or collecting any adjustment or recovery for Medicaid benefits correctly paid, effective on enactment.
Requires states to withdraw any existing recovery lien within 90 days and notify each affected person or legal representative that the lien is gone.

analysis.who_pays: State Medicaid programs, which lose the recovery revenue, and the Medicaid program overall, since care costs are no longer partially repaid from estates — pressure that could fall back on other Medicaid funding or taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: States lose recouped payments that currently offset Medicaid spending on long-term care, which could add budget pressure on state and federal Medicaid funding.

The bill sweeps out all recovery for correctly paid benefits with no transition period beyond the 90-day lien withdrawal, ending a policy intended to prevent wealthy estates from passing care costs to the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help is real and immediate for families facing liens on inherited homes, and the people affected are rarely the wealthy — estate recovery primarily reaches modest estates, which is why the family home is the main asset at stake. The cost is a revenue loss for state Medicaid programs that today is quietly repaid out of heirs' pockets. The trade-off is reasonable, but the bill would be stronger if it addressed where the lost revenue comes from.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 6, 2026 by Rep. Schakowsky.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill would repeal the federal mandate that states operate Medicaid Estate Recovery Programs and limit liens on Medicaid beneficiaries' property.
It directs states to withdraw existing liens within 90 days of enactment and notify affected individuals or their legal representatives.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained from the outcome yet: state Medicaid programs keep their authority to pursue estates and liens, and families remain exposed to recovery claims while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; recovery rules stand

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in January 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing or markup scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 24 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, though no one has voted against the bill either.

industries.note: States would lose the estate-recovery money they currently recoup from deceased beneficiaries' estates, including claims against family homes. The bill leaves open how states would backfill that revenue.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care providers
industries.note: Providers are paid the same either way; recovery only claws money back after death, so ending it neither cuts nor adds provider revenue directly. Indirectly, unrecovered care costs add budget pressure to Medicaid programs those providers depend on.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors from the majority party and no committee action two months after referral, the bill's realistic path is to remain in committee and expire at the end of the 119th Congress, unless the committee schedules a hearing on estate recovery or a companion effort gains traction.
